en: Majjhima Nikāya 66:
The Simile of the Quail Thus have I heard:
On one occasion the Blessed One was staying among the Aṅguttarāpas at a market town of theirs called Āpaṇa.
Then, in the morning, the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered Āpaṇa for alms.
Having walked for alms in Āpaṇa, after his meal, returning from his alms round, he approached a certain grove for his midday rest.
Having entered that grove, he sat down at the foot of a certain tree for his midday rest.
The Venerable Udāyī, having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl and robe, entered Āpaṇa for alms.
Having walked for alms in Āpaṇa, after his meal and returning from his almsround, he approached that grove for his midday rest.
Having entered that grove, he sat down at the foot of a certain tree for his midday rest.
Then, as the Venerable Udāyī was alone in seclusion, this reflection arose in his mind:
"The Blessed One has indeed removed from us many things that lead to suffering; the Blessed One has indeed bestowed upon us many things that lead to happiness."
“Indeed, the Blessed One has removed for us many unwholesome states; indeed, the Blessed One has brought about for us many wholesome states.
Then, in the evening, the Venerable Udāyī emerged from seclusion and approached the Blessed One.
Having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the Venerable...
Udāyī said this to the Blessed One:
“Here, Bhante, while I was alone in seclusion, this reflection arose in my mind:
‘The Blessed One has indeed removed for us many things that lead to suffering; the Blessed One has indeed brought about for us many things that lead to happiness.’”
‘The Blessed One has indeed removed for us many unwholesome states; the Blessed One has indeed brought about for us many wholesome states.
For previously, Bhante, we used to eat both in the evening, in the morning, and during the day at the improper time.
But there was a time, Bhante, when the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Come now, bhikkhus, you should abandon this eating at improper times during the day.
At this, venerable sir, I felt a change of heart and a sense of dejection:
“Even that exquisite food, both hard and soft, which faithful householders give us during the day at the wrong time—the Blessed One tells us to abandon it; the Sugata tells us to relinquish it!”
"Venerable sir, it was out of regard for the Blessed One, out of affection, reverence, shame, and fear of wrongdoing that we abandoned that daytime meal at the improper time.
Venerable sir, we eat both in the evening and in the morning.
Now, venerable sir, there was a time when the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:"
‘Come now, bhikkhus, abandon this eating at night, which is outside the proper time.
At that, venerable sir, there arose in me a sense of change and dejection:
‘The Blessed One tells us to abandon even that meal of the two which is considered more refined; the Sugata tells us to relinquish even that.’”
“Bhante, once in the past, a certain man having obtained some soup during the day said:
‘Come now, set this aside; we shall all eat it together in harmony this evening.
For whatever preparations there are, Bhante, they are all for the night; few are for the day.”
"Venerable sir, it was out of love for the Blessed One, respect for him, and considering our sense of shame and moral dread that we have thus abandoned that nocturnal meal at the wrong time.
Formerly, venerable sir, when monks were walking for alms in the thick darkness of the night,
they would fall into cesspools, fall into drains, climb over thorn-hedges, and even mount sleeping cows."
They encounter even young men, both those who have performed their duties and those who have not; even women invite them with what is not the true Dhamma.
Once in the past, venerable sir, I was walking for alms in the thick darkness of the night.
Then, venerable sir, a certain woman saw me through a gap in the doorway while she was washing a vessel.
Seeing me, she was terrified and cried out:
“Alas, a demon has come upon me!
When this was said, venerable sir, I said this to that woman:
“Sister, I am not a *pisāca*;
I am a monk standing for alms.
“The monk’s mother is dead; the monk’s father is dead.”
“It would be better for you, bhikkhu, to have your belly cut open with a sharp butcher’s knife than that you should wander for alms for the sake of your belly in the thick darkness of the night.
Venerable sir, as I recollect this, it occurs to me:
“The Blessed One has indeed removed from us many things that lead to suffering; the Blessed One has indeed bestowed upon us many things that lead to happiness.”
“The Blessed One has indeed removed for us many unwholesome states; the Blessed One has indeed brought about for us many wholesome states.
“In the same way, Udāyin, there are certain foolish men here who, when told by me, ‘Abandon this,’ say:
‘But what is the point of this trivial, petty thing? This ascetic is merely being overly fastidious.’”
They do not abandon that very thing and they display lack of confidence toward me.
For those monks who desire training, Udāyi, this becomes a powerful bond, a firm bond, a lasting bond, an undecayed bond—a massive, heavy yoke.
Just as a little quail bird, Udāyi, bound by a fetter of rotten creepers, meets its destruction, capture, or death right there.
Now, Udāyi, if someone were to say this:
“That by which that little female quail, bound with a bond of rotten creepers, meets with slaughter, capture,
or death right there— that is indeed her weak bond, her fragile bond, her putrid bond.”
“Is he speaking rightly, Udāyi, when he says: ‘Bondage is substantial, bondage is solid’?
“No, indeed, Bhante.”
“Venerable sir, that fetter by which the little quail bird is bound to the rotten creeper— there indeed it awaits its slaughter,
captivity, or death— is for her a powerful fetter, a firm fetter, a stable fetter,
a non-rotten fetter; it is a thick, solid block.”
“In the same way, Udāyi, here certain foolish men, when told by me, ‘Abandon this,’ say:
‘But what is there in this that is so trifling, so insignificant, that this ascetic would even shave it off?
They neither abandon that thing, nor do they place their trust in me.
“Udāyin, for those monks who desire training, that becomes a powerful bond, a firm bond, a stable bond, an undecayed bond, a massive, heavy yoke.
But here, Udāyin, some sons of good family, when told by me, ‘Abandon this,’ say:
‘What is this trifling, insignificant thing to be abandoned of which the Blessed One speaks as something to be abandoned, and of which the Sugata speaks as something to be relinquished?’”
They abandon that very thing and do not harbor resentment toward me.
And those monks who desire training, having abandoned it, dwell free from anxiety, with hair lying flat, subsisting on what others give, with minds like deer.
For them, Udāyi, that bond is weak, that bond is feeble, that bond is putrid, that bond is coreless.
"Just as, Udāyi, a king’s elephant— possessing tusks like chariot poles, well-born, of noble breed, and accustomed to the fray—
when bound with strong leather thongs, merely bends its body slightly, then cuts and breaks those bonds and departs wherever it desires."
Now, Udāyi, if someone were to say this: ‘When that royal elephant—
possessed of tusks as long as chariot-poles, well-bred, noble, and accustomed to battle— is bound with strong leather thongs and bonds,
he merely bends his body slightly, and having severed and burst those bonds apart, [he goes] where— ’
“Surely he would depart, for sensual desire is his powerful bond, a firm bond, a lasting bond,
an undecayed bond, a thick one, a massive log.
“Would he be speaking rightly, Udāyin, if he were to say that?”
“Certainly not, Bhante. For when that royal elephant— possessed of tusks as long as chariot-poles, noble, well-bred, and accustomed to battle—
is bound with strong leather thongs, he merely bends his body slightly, snaps those bonds, and tears them apart.”
“Whatever it is that one departs from at will, that indeed is his weak bond... [and so on] ...that is a coreless bond.
“In the same way, Udāyi, here some sons of good family, when told by me, ‘Abandon this,’ say this:
‘But what is this trifling, insignificant thing to be abandoned, for the abandoning of which the Blessed One speaks, for the relinquishing of which the Sugata speaks?’”
They abandon that very thing and do not harbor resentment toward me.
And those monks who desire training, having abandoned it, dwell free from anxiety, with hair lying flat, subsisting on what is given by others, with minds like deer.
For them, Udāyin, that bond is weak, that bond is feeble, that bond is putrid, that bond is coreless.
"Just as, Udāyi, there might be a man who was poor, destitute, and indigent;

he would have a single hut that was dilapidated and ruined, barely fit for crows, and not at all handsome; a single worn-out ragged blanket, not at all handsome; a single pot with a meager supply of grain, not at all handsome; and a single wife, not at all handsome.
Then he might see a monk who had come to a monastery, whose hands and feet were well-washed, who had eaten pleasing food, and who was sitting in the cool shade, devoted to higher mental training."
It might occur to him:
“How happy indeed is the state of a recluse! How healthy indeed is the state of a recluse!
It would truly be good for me to shave off my hair and beard, don saffron robes, and go forth from the household life into homelessness.”
Thus, he would not be able— having abandoned one dilapidated and ruined little house that was not of the finest quality,
having abandoned one dilapidated and ruined bed-cover that was not of the finest quality, having abandoned the grain stored in one jar that was not of the finest quality,
and having abandoned one wife who was not of the finest quality— to shave off his hair and beard and don the saffron robes.
...having clothed himself in robes, to go forth from the home life into homelessness.
Now, Udāyi, if someone were to say this:
‘The man who was bound by those bonds was not able [to escape] even a single dilapidated, ruinous little hut that crows were tearing apart—’”
Having abandoned exquisite forms, he might go forth from the home life into homelessness, wearing a single tattered and worn-out rag-robe;
having abandoned exquisite grain, he might carry a single jar of mixed grain; having abandoned exquisite wealth, he might possess a single coin;
and having shaved off his hair and beard and donned saffron robes, he might go forth from the home life into homelessness.
“Is he speaking rightly, Udāyī, when he says: ‘For that is his weak bond, his feeble bond, his putrid bond, his pithless bond’?
“Certainly not, Bhante.”
“Venerable sir, this man, bound by fetters, was unable to leave behind even one dilapidated and ruined little hut, not to mention anything more substantial;
he was unable to leave behind even one worn-out and tattered blanket, not to mention anything more substantial;

he was unable to leave behind even the grain stored in a single jar, not to mention anything more substantial; he was unable to leave behind even a single wife, not to mention anything more substantial.”
“Having shaved off hair and beard, having donned saffron robes, they go forth from the home life into homelessness;
for that is his powerful bond, his firm bond, his lasting bond, his non-rotting bond—bulky and heavy.
“In the same way, Udāyi, there are certain foolish men here who, when told by me, ‘Abandon this,’ they say this:”
‘But what is this insignificant, trivial thing for which this ascetic has shaved his head?
They do not abandon that very thing and harbor distrust toward me.
For those monks who desire training, Udāyi, that becomes a powerful bond, a firm bond, a lasting bond, an undecayed bond, a massive, heavy yoke.
"Just as, Udāyi, a householder or a householder’s son who is wealthy, possessing great riches and vast enjoyments,
has an accumulation of many heaps of coins, an accumulation of many heaps of grain, an accumulation of many heaps of fields,
an accumulation of many heaps of lands, an accumulation of many groups of wives, and an accumulation of many groups of male and female slaves;
Suppose he were to see a bhikkhu who has gone to a monastery, who has washed his hands and feet, who has eaten pleasing food, and is sitting in the cool shade, devoted to the higher mind.
It would occur to him:
"How happy indeed is this state of recluseship! How healthy indeed is this state of recluseship!"
‘It would indeed be well for me to shave off my hair and beard, don saffron robes, and go forth from the home life into homelessness.
He might then be able to abandon many groups of coins, many groups of grain, many groups of fields,
many groups of dwellings, many groups of wives, and many groups of slaves.
Having abandoned [them], having abandoned many groups of female slaves, having shaved off hair and beard, and having donned saffron-colored robes,
he went forth from the household life into homelessness.
Now, Udāyi, if someone were to say this:
"By whatever bonds that householder or householder’s son is bound, he is able— having abandoned many heaps of gold,
having abandoned many heaps of grain, having abandoned many fields, having abandoned many dwellings, having abandoned many wives,
and having abandoned many groups of male and female slaves— to depart."
‘Having shaved off hair and beard, and having donned saffron-colored robes, he should go forth from the home life into homelessness;
for that is his powerful bond, his firm bond, his enduring bond,
his non-putrid bond, his massive, heavy yoke.’”
“Would he, Udāyi, speaking correctly, speak thus?
“No, indeed, Bhante.
For by whatever bonds that householder or householder’s son is bound, he is able [to produce] many heaps of coins.”
Having abandoned them— having abandoned many groups of grain, having abandoned many groups of fields, having abandoned many groups of dwellings, having abandoned many groups of wives,
having abandoned many groups of male slaves, and having abandoned many groups of female slaves—
he shaves off his hair and beard, puts on saffron robes, and goes forth from the home life into homelessness.
“For that is his weak bond, his feeble bond, his putrid bond, his coreless bond.
“In the same way, Udāyi, when certain sons of good family here are told by me, ‘Abandon this,’ they say:
‘But what is this trifling, insignificant thing to be abandoned of which the Blessed One speaks as something to be abandoned, and of which the Sugata speaks as something to be relinquished?’”
They abandon that very thing and do not harbor resentment toward me.
And those monks who desire training, having abandoned it, dwell free from anxiety, with hair lying flat, subsisting on what others give, with minds like deer.
For them, Udāyi, that bond is weak, that bond is feeble, that bond is putrid, that bond is coreless.
"Udāyi, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world.
What are the four?
Here, Udāyi, a certain person practices for the abandoning of acquisitions and for the relinquishing of acquisitions."

When that person is practicing for the abandoning of acquisitions and for the relinquishing of acquisitions, thoughts associated with acquisitions still arise within them. They tolerate those thoughts;
they do not abandon them, do not dispel them, do not bring them to an end, and do not cause them to cease.
It is such a person, Udāyi, that I call "bound," not "unbound."
For what reason?
Because, Udāyi, I have perceived a difference in the faculties regarding this person.
Here, Udāyi, a certain person practices for the abandoning of acquisitions and for the relinquishing of acquisitions.
When that person is practicing for the abandoning of acquisitions and for the relinquishing of acquisitions, thoughts associated with acquisitions still assail him.
He does not tolerate them; he abandons them, dispels them, brings them to an end, and makes them non-existent.
Udāyi, this person too, I say, is "bound," not "released."
For what reason?
Because, Udāyi, I have perceived a difference in the faculties regarding this person.
Here, Udāyi, a certain person practices for the abandoning of acquisitions and for the relinquishing of acquisitions.

When he has thus practiced for the abandoning of acquisitions and for the relinquishing of acquisitions, occasionally and for a moment, through lapse of mindfulness, memories and intentions associated with acquisitions may still arise.
But the arising of his mindfulness is slow, Udāyin.
Yet he quickly abandons them, dispels them, brings them to an end, and makes them non-existent.
"Just as if, Udāyi, a man were to drop two or three drops of water into an iron cauldron heated all day long;
slow, Udāyi, would be the falling of those water drops. Yet they would very quickly reach exhaustion and disappearance.
Even so, Udāyi, here a certain person practices for the abandoning of acquisitions and for the relinquishing of acquisitions."

When one who has entered upon the practice for the abandoning of acquisitions and the relinquishing of acquisitions is, from time to time, assailed by memories and intentions associated with acquisitions due to a lapse of mindfulness,
the arising of mindfulness is slow,
Udāyin. Yet he quickly abandons them, dispels them, brings them to an end, and makes them non-existent.
“Udāyin, I also say of this person that he is ‘bound,’ not ‘released.
Why is that? Because, Udāyin, I have perceived a diversity of faculties in this person.”
"Furthermore, Udāyi, here a certain person, having understood that 'acquisition is the root of suffering,' becomes free from acquisition and is liberated through the destruction of acquisition.
This person, Udāyi, I call 'detached,' not 'bound.'"
For what reason?
Because, Udāyi, I have perceived a difference in their faculties regarding this person.
These, Udāyi, are the four types of persons found existing in the world.
There are, Udāyi, these five cords of sensual pleasure.
Which five?

Forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, pleasing, dear, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust; [sounds cognizable by the ear... [odors cognizable by the nose... [flavors cognizable by the tongue... [tangibles cognizable by the body that are desirable, lovely, pleasing, dear, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust.]
Sounds cognizable by the ear … [and so on] … odors cognizable by the nose … flavors cognizable by the tongue …
Tangible objects cognizable by the body that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual pleasure, and provocative of lust.
These, Udāyi, are the five cords of sensual pleasure.
Whatever happiness and joy arise in dependence on these five cords of sensual pleasure—this, Udāyi, is called...

The pleasure of sensual desires, the pleasure of filth, the pleasure of worldlings, the pleasure of the ignoble—this should not be cultivated, should not be developed, and should not be practiced frequently;
"one should fear this pleasure," I say.
Here, Udāyin, secluded from sensual desires... [a bhikkhu] enters and dwells in the first jhāna.
With the stilling of applied and sustained thought... he enters and dwells in the second jhāna;
with the fading away of rapture... he enters and dwells in the third jhāna;
and with the abandoning of pleasure... he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna.

This is called the happiness of renunciation, the happiness of seclusion, the happiness of peace, the happiness of enlightenment—it is to be cultivated, developed, and practiced frequently; “one should not fear this happiness,” I say.
Here, Udāyin, a bhikkhu, quite secluded from sensual pleasures... [as above] ...enters and dwells in the first jhāna;
this, Udāyin, I call a state of agitation.
And what, in this case, is the movement?
Whatever discursive thoughts and evaluations have not yet ceased—this, in this case, is the movement.
Here, Āḷāra Kālāma, with the subsiding of discursive thought and evaluation... [as before] ...a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the second jhāna.
"Udāyi, this too, I say, is a state of agitation.
And what therein is the state of agitation?
That very rapture and pleasure which has not yet ceased—this, I say, is the state of agitation therein."
"Udāyi, when a bhikkhu, with the fading away of rapture... enters and dwells in the third jhāna;
this too, Udāyi, I call a state of agitation.
And what is the agitation there?"
Whatever equanimity and pleasure remains unceased therein—that, Udāyi, is the "movement" therein.
Here, Udāyi, with the abandoning of pleasure... [as before] ...a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna;
this, Udāyi, I call "non-movement."
“Udāyi, here a bhikkhu, quite secluded from sensual pleasures … enters and dwells in the first jhāna.
This, Udāyi, I call ‘a fire’; I say ‘abandon it,’ I say ‘transcend it.
And what is its transcendence? [The second jhāna.]”
"Udāyi, when a bhikkhu, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought... enters and dwells in the second jhāna, this is his transcendence.
This too, Udāyi, I call 'a fire'; I say, 'Abandon it! I say, 'Transcend it! And what is its transcendence?"
"Udāyi, when a bhikkhu, with the fading away of rapture... enters and dwells in the third jhāna, this is his transcendence.
This too, Udāyi, I call 'a fire'; I say, 'Abandon it! I say, 'Transcend it! And what is its transcendence?"
“Udāyi, when a bhikkhu, with the abandoning of pleasure … [as above] … enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, this is his surmounting.
This too, Udāyi, I call a ‘flame’; I say, ‘Abandon it! I say, ‘Surmount it!
And what is its surmounting?

In this regard, Udāyi, when a bhikkhu, through the complete surmounting of perceptions of form, the disappearance of perceptions of sensory impact, and non-attention to perceptions of diversity, enters and dwells in the base of infinite space, thinking, "Space is infinite"—this is his surmounting.
And this too, Udāyi, I call a "flame"; I say, "Abandon it," and I say, "Surmount it."
And what is its transcendence?

Here, Udāyi, a bhikkhu, having completely transcended the base of infinite space, enters and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness, thinking, "Consciousness is infinite. This is its transcendence.
This too, Udāyi, I call a "flame"; I say, "Abandon it," and I say, "Transcend it."
And what is its transcendence?
Here, Udāyi, a bhikkhu, by completely transcending the base of infinite consciousness, thinking "there is nothing," enters and dwells in the base of nothingness. This is its transcendence.
This too, Udāyi, I call a "fire"; I say "abandon it" and I say "transcend it."
And what is its transcendence?
Here, Udāyi, a bhikkhu, by completely transcending the base of nothingness, enters and dwells in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; this is its transcendence.
This too, Udāyi, I call “a fire”; I say, “Abandon it! and I say, “Transcend it!”
And what is its transcendence?
Here, Udāyi, a bhikkhu, by completely transcending the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, enters and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling; this is its transcendence.
Thus, Udāyi, I speak of the abandoning even of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
“Udāyin, do you recognize that fetter—whether subtle or gross—the abandoning of which I do not speak?
“No, indeed, Bhante.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
The Venerable Udāyī was uplifted and rejoiced in the words spoken by the Blessed One.
The Sixth Discourse, the Simile of the Quail, is finished.
